source.title: Primary School Education Curriculum Design — Science & Technology, Grade 6
source.notes: Read in full via the Read tool (no pages param). ISBN 978-9914-724-90-5, First Published 2017, Revised 2024. Grade 6 is Upper Primary, NOT Junior School — the subject is called 'Science & Technology' (not 'Integrated Science', which starts Grade 7). Only 3 strands / 8 sub-strands / 120 total suggested lessons — the smallest Science curriculum design mined so far, which is why per-sub-strand depth (pool size, kind variety, Bloom's tier) matters even more than usual to avoid feeling thin.

subStrands.name: 1.1 Fungi
specificLearningOutcomes: Identify common fungi in the environment
Describe the importance of fungi in nature
Appreciate the importance of fungi in the economy
keyInquiryQuestions: How is fungi important in nature?
learningExperiences: Use print and non-print materials to search for images of common fungi (mushrooms, toadstool, puff balls, yeast and moulds) and share findings with peers
Take a walk in the school compound and the adjacent environment to observe and identify different types of fungi
Grow moulds on available food materials, observe and share with peers
Use print and non-print materials to search for information on the economic importance of moulds, yeast and mushrooms (food, fermentation, health and medicine), record and discuss with peers
linkedLearningAreas: Agriculture and Nutrition — economic importance of fungi links to food production
scopeNotes: exclude: scientific names of fungi not required
exclude: details on application of fungi in food processing not required
include: precautions and safe disposal of wastes when handling fungi (from the Note under Suggested Learning Experiences)
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Rubric rewards describing importance of fungi 'correctly and comprehensively' at Exceeds tier — the economic importance list (food, fermentation, health, medicine) should all be individually recallable, not just 'fungi are useful'.
pertinentContemporaryIssues: Environmental conservation (safe waste disposal when handling fungi)

subStrands.name: 1.2 Invertebrates
specificLearningOutcomes: Identify common invertebrates in the environment
Practise precautions in handling invertebrates
Describe the general characteristics of invertebrates
Outline the economic importance of invertebrates
Appreciate the importance of invertebrates in nature
keyInquiryQuestions: What are the common features of invertebrates?
learningExperiences: Walk around the school compound, observe and identify common invertebrates (insects; spiders, ticks and mites; millipedes and centipedes; snails and slugs; worms; sea invertebrates — octopus, starfish and crabs), record and share with peers
Discuss with peers the safety precautions applied when handling invertebrates
Use print and non-print materials to search for information on general characteristics of invertebrates
Explore the school compound and the adjacent environment to identify different invertebrates and their characteristics; practise safety precautions in handling invertebrates
Make an inventory of common invertebrates in their locality
Discuss the economic importance of invertebrates (food, pollination, soil aeration, pests, transmission of diseases)
linkedLearningAreas: Agriculture and Nutrition — transmission of diseases links to communicable diseases
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Rubric's Exceeds tier for economic importance asks for 'example(s) from the locality' — real-world, localized examples are explicitly rewarded, not generic textbook statements.

subStrands.name: 1.3 Human circulatory system
specificLearningOutcomes: Identify main parts of the human circulatory system
Describe functions of main parts of the human circulatory system
Outline the symptoms and prevention of common health conditions of the human circulatory system
Develop a routine plan for maintaining a healthy circulatory system
Appreciate the importance of a healthy circulatory system
keyInquiryQuestions: What is the human circulatory system made up of?
What measures enhance a healthy human circulatory system?
learningExperiences: Search for information on the main parts of the human circulatory system (heart, blood vessels and blood) and share findings with peers
Use locally available materials to model the human circulatory system
Use online interactive platforms or digital images or writing materials to illustrate main parts of the human circulatory system
Search for information on parts of the heart (auricles, ventricles and vessels) and their functions, record and share findings
Discuss the functions of the main blood vessels in the human body (arteries, veins and capillaries)
Discuss the components of blood and their functions (red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets)
Search for information on the symptoms and prevention of common health conditions of the human circulatory system (hardening of arteries, high blood pressure and heart attack) and share findings
Discuss ways of maintaining a healthy human circulatory system
Develop a routine plan for maintaining a healthy circulatory system (to include drinking plenty of water, physical activities and healthy eating)
linkedLearningAreas: Creative Arts — modelling the human circulatory system links to modelling in Creative Arts and Sports
scopeNotes: exclude: details of different blood vessels and parts of the body not needed
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Separate rubric rows exist for (a) describing functions of main parts and (b) developing a routine plan — a skill must cover BOTH structure/function facts AND an applied routine-plan behaviour, not just anatomy recall.

subStrands.name: 2.1 Change of State
specificLearningOutcomes: Identify the changes of state when substances are heated or cooled
Describe the applications of the change of state of matter in everyday life
Appreciate the applications of change of state of matter in day-to-day life
keyInquiryQuestions: How is change of state of matter important in day-to-day life?
learningExperiences: Brainstorm the meaning of change of state of matter
Carry out activities to demonstrate change of state of matter: melting, evaporation, sublimation, deposition, condensation and freezing (all 6 named transitions)
Discuss the applications of change of state of matter in everyday life
Use digital or print media to search for information on what happens when matter is heated or cooled
linkedLearningAreas: Agriculture and Nutrition — evaporation as a process of drying clothes and cereals
scopeNotes: include: observe safety while heating substances to avoid fires and burns
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Exceeds tier explicitly rewards identifying changes 'giving examples from locality' and Meets tier requires 'at least four' of the six named transitions — sublimation and deposition (the two least everyday-obvious ones) must not be dropped in favour of only melting/freezing/evaporation/condensation.
pertinentContemporaryIssues: Socio-economic issues (Environmental Education) — reusing wax/plastic to save cost
projects: Make candles using waste candle wax or beeswax

subStrands.name: 2.2 Composition of Air
specificLearningOutcomes: Identify the components of air
Outline uses of the different components of air
Explain the effects of air pollution in the environment
Describe methods of reducing air pollution in the environment
Appreciate the need for clean air in day-to-day life
keyInquiryQuestions: How does air pollution affect the environment?
learningExperiences: Brainstorm on the meaning of air and its constituents
Draw a pie chart showing percentage composition of components of air
Carry out an activity to investigate the presence of oxygen in air collaboratively (use a burning candle)
Discuss the uses of the different components of air
Brainstorm on the meaning of air pollution
Explore the school and neighbourhood to identify air pollutants
Discuss the effects of air pollution on the environment
Identify and discuss methods of reducing air pollution
Use digital or print media to search for more information on the effects of air pollution
linkedLearningAreas: Mathematics — drawing a pie chart showing percentage composition of components of air
scopeNotes: include: observe safety precautions in air-polluted environments (dust masks, goggles, overcoats)
subStrands.assessmentSignal: The Mathematics cross-link plus the explicit 'draw a pie chart' learning experience means a pie-chart VisualSpec for the ~78% nitrogen / 21% oxygen / 1% other-gases split is curriculum-endorsed, not an invented visual.
pertinentContemporaryIssues: Socio-economic and environmental issues (environmental education and climate change)
projects: Make posters on common air pollutants, dangers of air pollution and ways of controlling air pollution

subStrands.name: 3.1 Light
specificLearningOutcomes: Demonstrate the movement of light through materials
Draw ray diagrams of images formed in plane mirrors
Illustrate the formation of shadows and eclipses in nature
Describe the formation of rainbow in nature
Appreciate the importance of movement of light in everyday life
learningExperiences: Carry out activities to show the movement of light through different materials (transparent, translucent and opaque)
Perform an experiment to show reflection of light in plane mirrors (laws of reflection)
Locate and illustrate images formed in plane mirrors and discuss their characteristics
Carry out activities to demonstrate and illustrate the formation of shadows and eclipses (solar & lunar eclipses)
Use digital or print media to search for more information on movement of light through materials, image formation in plane mirrors, formation of shadows, eclipses and rainbow in nature
Discuss the applications of movement of light through different media (mirrors, periscope, kaleidoscope, lenses, magnifying glass, hand lens, mirage, rainbow)
linkedLearningAreas: Home Science — the concept of ray of light in lighting up the home
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Separate rubric row exists specifically for 'ability to illustrate the formation of shadows and eclipses in nature' with 'correctly and labels' at Exceeds — a shadow/eclipse diagram needs actual labelled parts (light source, opaque object, umbra), not just a verbal description.
pertinentContemporaryIssues: Socio-economic issues (safety and security when handling mirrors during experiments)
projects: Make a functional periscope using locally available resources

subStrands.name: 3.2 Levers as simple machines
specificLearningOutcomes: Identify common levers used in day-to-day life
Describe parts of a lever as used in making work easier
Classify levers into the three classes
Demonstrate the use of levers in making work easier
Appreciate the use of levers in making work easier
keyInquiryQuestions: How are levers used in day to day life?
learningExperiences: Brainstorm on the meaning of levers as simple machines
Work collaboratively to identify parts of a lever (fulcrum/pivot, effort, load)
Carry out activities to group levers into the three classes (first, second and third class levers)

Carry out activities to demonstrate the use of common levers as simple machines: a hole punch, pliers, scissors, a see-saw, wheelbarrow, bottle openers, nail clippers, a nutcracker, shovel, fishing rod, kitchen tongs and tweezers (12 named examples)
Use digital or print media to search for information on how levers make work easier in day-to-day life
linkedLearningAreas: Agriculture and Nutrition — application of the principle of levers in farm tools, use of cutlery, spoons and bottle openers
Creative Arts — applying the concept of simple levers while playing on a see-saw
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Ability-to-demonstrate rubric rewards 'correctly and innovatively' at Exceeds — beyond classifying the 12 named tools, a skill should require reasoning about WHY a given class arrangement makes work easier for that specific tool, not just rote class-1/2/3 labels.
pertinentContemporaryIssues: Citizenship education (care and protection of one another during experiments)
projects: Make and use a beam balance from locally available materials

subStrands.name: 3.3 Slopes as simple machines
specificLearningOutcomes: Identify types of slopes used as simple machines
Demonstrate how a slope makes work easier in day-to-day life
Appreciate the use of slopes in everyday life
keyInquiryQuestions: How are slopes used in everyday life?
learningExperiences: Discuss the meaning of slope as a simple machine (inclined plane)
Give practical examples on where slopes are used to make work easier around the school environment (ladders, ramps, staircase, road winding uphill, wedge, roofs, loading a lorry)
Discuss how slopes are used to make work easier in day-to-day life
Carry out activities to show how slopes make work easier

Use digital media to search for information on how slopes make work easier (elevators/lifts, escalators/moving stairs, staircase, ladders, cableways, ramps, road winding uphill, wedge, roofs, loading a lorry)
Discuss the importance of use of slopes in day-to-day life
linkedLearningAreas: Agriculture and Nutrition — the concept of slope in the use of farm tools, equipment and machinery
subStrands.assessmentSignal: The Core Competencies box explicitly names 'Critical thinking and problem solving' — per RIGOR-STANDARDS.md this sub-strand requires at least one Analyze-or-Evaluate-tier branch (e.g. comparing a steep vs gentle slope's effort/distance trade-off), not only Remember-tier slope-type identification.
projects: Make a simple slope for use in school or at home using locally available materials
